courses.title: Internal Medicine IV: Neurology, Haematology and Rheumatology
courses.description: Stroke, epilepsy, headache and neuropathies; anaemia, sickle cell disease and haematological malignancies; and arthritis and connective tissue diseases.

topics.title: Stroke
topics.summary: Types, risk factors, acute assessment and management, and secondary prevention.

material.heading: Presentation and assessment
material.body: Stroke is a sudden focal (sometimes global) neurological deficit of vascular origin lasting > 24 hours or causing death; a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) resolves within 24 hours (usually within an hour) with no infarction — a warning sign. In Nigeria, stroke patients are relatively young and haemorrhagic stroke is more common (about 30–40%) than in high-income countries; hypertension is the dominant risk factor, followed by diabetes, dyslipidaemia, smoking, atrial fibrillation, sickle cell disease (in children) and HIV. Recognition: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time). Non-contrast CT brain is urgent to distinguish haemorrhage from infarction (infarcts may not be visible early). Assessment includes glucose (exclude hypoglycaemia), ECG, BP, swallow screen and NIHSS score. Clinical localisation: middle cerebral artery (contralateral face/arm weakness, aphasia if dominant, neglect if non-dominant), anterior cerebral (leg), posterior circulation (vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, crossed signs), lacunar (pure motor or sensory).

material.heading: Management
material.body: Ischaemic stroke: thrombolysis with IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset in eligible patients (after excluding haemorrhage; limited availability in Nigeria), mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion (few centres), aspirin 300 mg within 24–48 hours if not thrombolysed (after CT), stroke unit care, swallow assessment, DVT prevention, early mobilisation and rehabilitation. Blood pressure: avoid aggressive lowering in ischaemic stroke unless > 220/120 (or > 185/110 before thrombolysis). Intracerebral haemorrhage: lower systolic BP to about 140 mmHg, reverse anticoagulation, neurosurgical referral for cerebellar haemorrhage or hydrocephalus. Subarachnoid haemorrhage: sudden 'thunderclap' headache; CT then lumbar puncture (xanthochromia) if negative; nimodipine; aneurysm coiling or clipping. Secondary prevention: antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), statins, BP control, anticoagulation for AF, carotid endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis, and lifestyle change.
keyPoints: Don't lower BP aggressively in ischaemic stroke

topics.title: Epilepsy, Headache and Neuromuscular Disease
topics.summary: Seizure classification and management, headache syndromes, Parkinson's disease, neuropathy and myasthenia.

material.heading: Seizures and headache
material.body: Epilepsy affects about 1% of Nigerians and carries stigma (myths of contagion or spiritual causes). Seizures are focal (with or without impaired awareness, may evolve to bilateral tonic–clonic) or generalised (tonic–clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic). Causes in Nigeria include birth injury, febrile seizure complications, CNS infections (cerebral malaria, meningitis, neurocysticercosis), head trauma, stroke and tumours. Investigate with EEG and neuroimaging. Treatment: carbamazepine or lamotrigine for focal; valproate (not in women of childbearing potential), lamotrigine or levetiracetam for generalised; phenobarbital (affordable, WHO-recommended in resource-limited settings). Status epilepticus (seizure > 5 minutes or repeated without recovery): ABC, glucose, benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam or diazepam, buccal midazolam, rectal diazepam), repeat once, then phenytoin/levetiracetam/valproate/phenobarbital, then anaesthesia. Headache: tension-type (bilateral, band-like), migraine (unilateral, pulsating, with nausea, photophobia, aura; triptans; prophylaxis with propranolol, amitriptyline), cluster; red flags — thunderclap onset, fever and neck stiffness, papilloedema, new headache after 50, focal signs, immunosuppression.

material.heading: Movement and neuromuscular disorders
material.body: Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia with rigidity, rest tremor or postural instability; levodopa–carbidopa is most effective. Peripheral neuropathy: diabetic (commonest), HIV and antiretroviral-related, alcohol, B12 deficiency, leprosy, isoniazid, and konzo (spastic paraparesis from cyanide exposure in poorly processed cassava) and tropical ataxic neuropathy. Guillain–Barré syndrome: ascending flaccid paralysis and areflexia after infection; monitor vital capacity; IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and limb weakness) from acetylcholine-receptor antibodies; pyridostigmine, immunosuppression and thymectomy; myasthenic crisis needs ventilatory support. Spinal cord compression (metastases, TB — Pott's disease, trauma): back pain, leg weakness, sensory level and sphincter disturbance — urgent MRI and treatment. Motor neurone disease: mixed UMN and LMN signs without sensory loss.

topics.title: Anaemia and Sickle Cell Disease
topics.summary: Classification of anaemia, common causes in Nigeria, and adult sickle cell disease care.

material.heading: Anaemia
material.body: Anaemia (Hb < 13 g/dL men, < 12 non-pregnant women, < 11 pregnancy) is classified by MCV. Microcytic: iron deficiency (commonest — dietary, hookworm, menstrual and GI blood loss; low ferritin), thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease (sometimes). Normocytic: acute blood loss, chronic disease (HIV, TB, CKD, rheumatoid arthritis — ferritin normal/high), haemolysis, marrow failure. Macrocytic: vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, neurological signs — subacute combined degeneration), folate deficiency (pregnancy, haemolysis, poor diet), alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs (methotrexate, zidovudine). Haemolysis: raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin; causes include malaria, G6PD deficiency (oxidant drugs, fava beans), sickle cell disease, autoimmune haemolysis and transfusion reactions. Blood film is key. Treat the cause; oral iron (ferrous sulfate) for deficiency; transfuse only when necessary.

material.heading: Sickle cell disease in adults
material.body: Nigeria has the largest number of people with sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC, HbS-β-thalassaemia). Survival into adulthood is increasing. Acute complications: vaso-occlusive painful crises (triggers — infection, dehydration, cold, stress; treat with prompt analgesia including opioids, fluids, oxygen if hypoxic), acute chest syndrome (new pulmonary infiltrate with chest pain, fever, hypoxia — leading cause of death; antibiotics, oxygen, incentive spirometry, transfusion), stroke, splenic or hepatic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 — low reticulocytes), priapism, and infections (encapsulated organisms, Salmonella osteomyelitis). Chronic: avascular necrosis of the femoral head, leg ulcers, retinopathy (especially HbSC), nephropathy, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones and pregnancy complications. Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) increases HbF and reduces crises, acute chest syndrome and mortality — recommended widely; plus folic acid, malaria prophylaxis, vaccinations, penicillin prophylaxis in children, and genetic counselling. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (available in a few Nigerian centres) is curative.
keyPoints: Acute chest syndrome: leading cause of death

topics.title: Haematological Malignancies and Bleeding Disorders
topics.summary: Leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloma, and approach to bleeding and thrombosis.

material.heading: Haematological malignancies
material.body: Acute leukaemias (AML, ALL) present with bone marrow failure — anaemia, infections, bleeding — plus blasts on the blood film and > 20% blasts in marrow; ALL is commonest in children and AML in adults; acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) causes DIC and is treated urgently with ATRA. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR-ABL1 — Philadelphia chromosome): massive splenomegaly and high white cell count with left shift; imatinib (available in Nigeria through access programmes) transforms survival. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: elderly, lymphocytosis, smear cells. Lymphomas: Hodgkin (Reed–Sternberg cells, painless lymphadenopathy, B symptoms — fever, night sweats, weight loss) and non-Hodgkin (Burkitt lymphoma — jaw tumours in African children, EBV and malaria-associated, rapidly growing but highly chemosensitive; HIV-related lymphomas). Multiple myeloma (older adults, often black patients): bone pain and lytic lesions, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment (CRAB), paraprotein on serum electrophoresis, Bence Jones proteinuria.

material.heading: Bleeding and thrombosis
material.body: Approach to bleeding: platelet-type bleeding (petechiae, mucosal bleeding — thrombocytopenia, ITP, platelet dysfunction, von Willebrand disease) versus coagulation-factor bleeding (deep haematomas, haemarthroses — haemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX), X-linked, prolonged APTT). Tests: platelet count, PT/INR (extrinsic — warfarin, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency), APTT (intrinsic — haemophilia, heparin), fibrinogen and D-dimer. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (sepsis, obstetric complications — abruption, amniotic fluid embolism; snakebite; APL): low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT/APTT, high D-dimer; treat the cause and replace products. Venous thromboembolism (DVT and PE): risk factors include immobility, surgery, pregnancy and postpartum, cancer, oral contraceptives, and dehydration; Wells score and D-dimer guide testing (compression ultrasound, CTPA); treat with low-molecular-weight heparin then warfarin or a DOAC for at least 3 months. Warfarin overdose: vitamin K ± prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma; heparin: protamine.
keyPoints: DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, high D-dimer

topics.title: Rheumatology
topics.summary: Inflammatory arthritis, gout, SLE, and approach to joint pain.

material.heading: Arthritis
material.body: Approach to joint pain: number of joints (mono-, oligo-, polyarthritis), inflammatory (morning stiffness > 30 minutes, swelling, improves with activity) versus mechanical, and systemic features. Acute monoarthritis: septic arthritis must be excluded by joint aspiration (Staphylococcus aureus commonest; gonococcal in young sexually active adults; Salmonella in sickle cell) — urgent antibiotics and washout; gout (monosodium urate crystals — negatively birefringent needles; first MTP joint, precipitated by alcohol, diuretics, purine-rich foods; treat acute attacks with NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids; long-term urate-lowering with allopurinol, not started during the attack traditionally, with colchicine cover); pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate — positively birefringent rhomboids, knee in elderly). Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, erosions; start disease-modifying drugs early (methotrexate with folic acid — monitor FBC and LFTs; hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide; biologics). Osteoarthritis is the commonest arthritis (knees in obese older women).

material.heading: Connective tissue disease
material.body: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE — mostly young women, more severe in people of African descent): malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, nephritis, cytopenias, neuropsychiatric features; ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific), low complement in active disease. Treatment: hydroxychloroquine for all, steroids, and immunosuppressants (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis). Systemic sclerosis: skin thickening, Raynaud's phenomenon, interstitial lung disease, renal crisis. Vasculitides and polymyositis are less common. HIV is associated with reactive arthritis, psoriatic-type arthritis and other rheumatological problems. Reactive arthritis follows GI or genitourinary infection (arthritis, urethritis, conjunctivitis). Spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis) are HLA-B27-associated and relatively rare in West Africans.
